messages.content: What is the Higgs field and why does the Higgs boson matter?

The Standard Model of particle physics requires a mechanism to give fundamental particles mass without breaking the symmetry of the electroweak force. The Higgs mechanism (1964): a scalar field (the Higgs field) permeates all of space. Particles that interact with this field gain mass — the stronger the interaction, the more massive the particle. Photons don't interact with it (massless). Top quarks interact strongly (heaviest quark). The Higgs boson is the particle associated with this field — a quantum of the Higgs field, as the photon is a quantum of the electromagnetic field. Discovered at CERN's LHC in 2012 — the last particle predicted by the Standard Model to be confirmed experimentally.
What is quantum entanglement and why did Einstein call it 'spooky action at a distance'?

Quantum entanglement: when two particles interact in certain ways, their quantum states become correlated — measuring one instantly determines the corresponding property of the other, regardless of distance. Einstein called this 'spooky action at a distance' because it seemed to imply instantaneous influence across space — violating his conviction that nothing can travel faster than light. Resolution: entanglement doesn't transmit information faster than light. The correlation exists, but neither party can use it to send a message — the outcome of each measurement is random; the correlation only becomes apparent when both sets of results are compared (which requires classical communication). Bell's theorem and subsequent experiments (Aspect et al., 1982) confirmed entanglement is real and irreducible.
What is dark matter and what is the evidence for it?

Dark matter: non-luminous matter that interacts gravitationally but not electromagnetically (doesn't emit, absorb, or reflect light). Evidence: galaxy rotation curves (stars at the edges of galaxies orbit too fast for the visible mass — additional unseen mass must be present), gravitational lensing (light bends more around galaxy clusters than visible mass predicts), large-scale structure formation (galaxies form the pattern they do only if cold dark matter scaffolded the early universe). Dark matter comprises ~27% of the universe's energy content. Candidates: WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles), axions, primordial black holes. Despite extensive direct detection experiments, dark matter has never been directly observed — its nature remains one of physics' greatest open questions.
Explain special relativity and its consequences.

Special relativity (Einstein, 1905): the laws of physics are identical for all observers in uniform motion, and the speed of light in vacuum is constant for all observers regardless of the motion of the light source. Consequences: time dilation (moving clocks run slow — a clock on a fast-moving spacecraft ticks slower than one on Earth), length contraction (objects moving at high speed are shorter in the direction of motion as measured by a stationary observer), relativity of simultaneity (events simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in another), and mass-energy equivalence (E=mc² — mass and energy are interconvertible). At everyday speeds, effects are negligible. At 99.9% light speed, time dilation factor ~22x.
